definition: Chide means to scold gently; to voice mild disapproval.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word chide. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know chide should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The yoga teacher chided us for rushing the cooldown — one raised eyebrow and a soft 'again, slowly.'
Teasing is play, not correction — even gentler than chide, which does mean the disapproval.
Scold goes further than chide: real anger in the voice, where chide keeps its warmth.

To correct is to point out a fault neutrally, with no disapproving tone at all — just the fix, stated plainly. Chide adds mild, warm disapproval on top: the speaker really does mean the reproof, however gently it lands. A spell-checker corrects; a fond grandmother chides.

To reproach someone is to voice mild blame with hurt feelings in it — 'you might have called.' Chide carries affection instead of injury: the chider is not wounded, just gently steering someone back to form. A friend you let down reproaches you; an aunt who catches you slouching chides you.

Old English cidan left no other descendants: chide is its entire surviving family. Words that stayed home in English often come to us short, blunt, and single — unlike the Latin scolding words built from parts, like admonish and chastise on this unit's other cards.
Chide means to scold gently; to voice mild disapproval.
When the new hire signed his emails with just his initials, the office manager chided him in passing: 'We do full names here, friend.'
Chide is the gentlest word on the scolding shelf: mild disapproval voiced without anger, often with warmth still in it.
If voices rise or the correction goes on the record, you have left chide behind for its sterner cousins.
Chide is scolding with the affection left in — for grandmothers, coaches, and old friends.
If real anger enters, you have moved to admonish or berate (this unit); if there is no disapproval at all, it was only teasing.

My beekeeping mentor, Mrs.
Okafor, chided me the whole first summer — for rushing the smoker, for skipping gloves, for talking too loudly around the hives.
It never once felt like being told off.
She would shake her head, half-smiling, and say, 'Again, but slower this time.' The disapproval was real; she genuinely wanted the habits gone.
But there was no anger in it, and no scorekeeping.
When I finally cracked a frame, I braced for the storm.
It never came — just the head-shake, the smile, and a quieter 'slower.' Years on, I catch myself doing the same gentle scolding with my own students, right down to the half-smile.
